subject: Estimating g(0) for passive acoustic surveys

messages.author: 5f6af0654b8b4648
messages.subject: Estimating g(0) for passive acoustic surveys
parts:
Dear List



I am conducting Distance analysis on data collected during a passive
acoustic survey for harbour porpoises in the North Sea in November. We had
13 sightings during the survey and over 200 usable detections. I am now
looking into how to calculate the g(0) for this survey.



One way of calculating the g(0) which has been suggested to me by more
experienced scientists in Distance sampling is to compare the number of
sightings with the number of sightings which have detections (13 sightings,
7 of which have corresponding acoustic detections). This method provides me
with an estimate of g(0) around 0.46 which I believe is extremely low.



To me, this seems to ignore the fact that although only 7 of the 13
sightings had corresponding detections, we had 235 detections during this
time. Additionally being a winter survey in the North Sea, the sighting
conditions were very poor and very few of the sightings occurred in sea
states less than 3. Is there a way of including all the encounters (235+13)
and calculating the g(0) by the number of encounters that were missed (this
gives me a much higher g(0) value of around 0.9). To me this seems much more
accurate, as I would be worried that by using the other technique the end
abundance estimates would be overestimated, however as these are widely
different.



Any suggestions or guidance on this topic would be much appreciated.



Many thanks in advance,



Anna





Anna Cucknell

Marine Conservation Research Ltd.

Marine Conservation Research International

messages.author: 778abaa663647a33
messages.subject: Re: Estimating g(0) for passive acoustic surveys
parts:
It could be too low if there is negative dependence between visual and
acoustic detections which is very likely. Negative dependence means what
can be heard can't be seen and what can be seen can't be heard to some
degree. Typically with methods using dual visual observers the dependence
is positive which can mean g(0) estimate is too high. But with different
detection techniques the dependence can be negative. I believe this is
written up in a report on acoustic methods for marine mammal surveys that I
attended a number of years ago in San Diego.

regards --jeff
